claim: Meiji Jingu opens at sunrise and closes at sunset with free admission year-round; June hours are roughly 5:00 to 18:30.
quote: Earliest opening: 5:00 AM (May-August); Latest closing: 6:30 PM (June). Admission Cost: Free entry year-round.

claim: The Imperial Palace East Gardens are free and open 9:00-18:00 from April 15-Aug 31 but are closed every Monday and Friday.
quote: April 15 – August 31: 9:00–18:00 (entry until 17:30) ... closed on the following days and occasions: Every Monday and Friday ... The gardens are completely free to visit.

claim: Tokyo Skytree adult tickets start from JPY 1,800 for the Tembo Deck (350m) and JPY 3,000 for the combo with Tembo Galleria (450m).
quote: Tembo Deck (Floor 350) Adults (15+): From ¥1,800 ... Combo Ticket (Both Floors) Adults (15+): From ¥3,000 ... Children 5 and under: Free.

claim: Tokyo Skytree's last admission is one hour before closing and operating hours can change without notice.
quote: The last admission is one hour before closing ... Opening hours may change without prior notice.

claim: Senso-ji's main hall is open 6:00-17:00 (6:30 in winter), grounds are open 24 hours, and the buildings including the five-story pagoda are illuminated until 23:00 each night.
quote: The temple's main hall and amulet shops are open between 6:00 and 17:00 in summer, and from 6:30 until 17:00 in the wintertime ... Each night the temple buildings (including the famous five-story pagoda) are stunningly illuminated until 23:00.

claim: Senso-ji is Tokyo's oldest temple and attracts around 30 million worshippers annually, with the Kaminari-mon gate, Nakamise Street, main hall and five-story pagoda as the headline sights.
quote: Location: 2-3-1 Asakusa, Taito-ku, Tokyo 111-0032, Japan ... The temple attracts approximately 30 million worshippers annually ... Key Sites: Kaminari-mon Gate (main entrance), Nakamise Shopping Street, Main Hall (Kannondo Hall), Five-Storied Pagoda.

claim: Shibuya Sky's 46th floor outdoor SKY STAGE gives the best bird's-eye view of the Scramble Crossing, while free options include the Mark City pedestrian bridge and the Shibuya Tsutaya Starbucks second-floor windows.
quote: Shibuya Sky, located in the SHIBUYA SCRAMBLE SQUARE building, offers a breathtaking bird's-eye view from the 46th floor's outdoor observatory, the SKY STAGE ... the 2nd floor [Tsutaya Starbucks] has an area overlooking the Shibuya Scramble Crossing.

claim: Shibuya Sky adult tickets are JPY 3,000 before 14:59 and JPY 3,700 from 15:00 onwards, with sunset slots the most popular booking window.
quote: Adult tickets are 3,000 yen (before 14:59) or 3,700 yen (15:00 onwards), according to the official Tokyo travel guide.

claim: The Imperial Household Agency runs free 75-minute guided tours of the Imperial Palace inner grounds twice a day in English and Japanese, bookable online or by walk-up numbered ticket, with passport required.
quote: Imperial Household Agency runs its own free guided tour of the Inner Grounds — a roughly 75-minute walk ... running in English and Japanese, twice daily on the days it operates ... For the official guided tour, you need to bring your physical passport as it is required for registration.

claim: Meiji Shrine sits in a 70-hectare forest beside Harajuku Station and the optional Inner Garden costs JPY 500 while the Treasure Museum costs JPY 1,000.
quote: The shrine is free. The Inner Garden costs ¥500, and the Museum ¥1,000.

claim: Sensoji visits combine the outer Kaminari-mon gate, the 200+ metre Nakamise shopping street, a second gate, the main hall and five-story pagoda — typically 1-2 hours, best early morning or after dark to avoid daytime crowds.
quote: the outer gate, a 200+ meter shopping street (Nakamise), a second gate, main hall, five-story pagoda, and adjacent Asakusa Shrine — suggests allocating at least 1-2 hours for a thorough visit.

claim: Asakusa is 'where you'll find the Tokyo of old' — a historic, slightly crowded former pleasure district whose Senso-ji area has costumed rickshaw drivers and easy access to Kappabashi Kitchen Town.
quote: Asakusa is where you'll find the Tokyo of old; from the 7th century golden image of Kannon (the Buddhist Goddess of Mercy) enshrined in Senso-ji temple's main hall... Around the temple, costumed rickshaw drivers offer tours of the area.

claim: Senso-ji is illuminated from sunset to ~23:00 and evening visits see 70–80% fewer crowds than daytime peak, making after-dark the best window for photos and a quieter walk.
quote: Sensō-ji is lit up every evening from sunset until around 23:00, and the sight of the main hall, Kaminari-mon Gate, and the five-story pagoda emerging from the darkness is truly spectacular. Evening visits offer 70-80% fewer crowds compared to daytime peak hours.

claim: Ginza is Tokyo's premier upmarket shopping/dining district; the central Chuo Dori closes to traffic on weekend afternoons (noon–18:00, until 17:00 Oct–Mar), making weekend afternoon the ideal visit window via Ginza or Yurakucho stations.
quote: Ginza (銀座) is Tokyo's most famous upmarket shopping, dining and entertainment district... A visit is most pleasant on weekend afternoons when the central Chuo Dori street is closed to automobile traffic and become a large pedestrian zone. The road closure takes place from noon to 18:00.

claim: Akihabara is Tokyo's electronics/anime/manga district along Chuo Dori (closed to cars Sun 13:00–18:00); Akihabara Station is served by JR Yamanote, Keihin-Tohoku, Sobu, Tsukuba Express and Hibiya lines, and the Yodobashi Camera complex is the standout big-box anchor.
quote: Akihabara... is a district in central Tokyo that is famous for its many electronics shops... Hundreds of electronics shops... line the main Chuo Dori street... On Sundays, Chuo Dori, the main street through the district, is closed to car traffic from 13:00 to 18:00.

claim: Shinjuku is Tokyo's biggest entertainment/business hub anchored by the world's busiest station (2M+ daily passengers); Kabukicho is Japan's largest red-light district, Golden Gai packs 200+ tiny bars, and the free Tokyo Metropolitan Government 45F observatories deliver night skyline views.
quote: Shinjuku Station is the world's busiest railway station, handling more than two million passengers every day... [Kabukicho is] Japan's largest and wildest red light district... [Golden Gai is] a small, atmospheric nightlife district in Kabukicho packed with over 200 small bars and eateries.

claim: For Golden Gai, the recommended approach is 2–3 bars over the evening with 45–90 min per bar; many bars accept foreigners but cash-only is common and 'regulars only' signs should be respected.
quote: Choose two or three bars across the evening. Bar-hopping is the intended use of Golden Gai. Spending 45–90 minutes per bar is typical... Many establishments in Golden Gai prefer cash payments... Some bars post signs saying regulars only — respect these and move on.

claim: Harajuku's Takeshita Street (~400m) is the focal point of teen kawaii fashion, while parallel Omotesando — sometimes called Tokyo's Champs-Élysées — runs over twice as long and skews adult/luxury with flagship boutiques.
quote: Takeshita Street is a narrow, roughly 400 meter long street lined by shops, boutiques, cafes and fast food outlets targeting Tokyo's teenagers... Just south of Takeshita Dori and over twice its length is Omotesando, a broad, tree-lined avenue sometimes referred to as Tokyo's Champs-Elysees.

claim: Harajuku is the global birthplace of kawaii culture; access is via Harajuku Station on JR Yamanote (4 min from Shinjuku) or Meiji-jingumae on Tokyo Metro Chiyoda/Fukutoshin lines, and Meiji Shrine offers a quiet escape next door.
quote: Harajuku has a completely different, and global, appeal as a birthplace of kawaii (cute) culture... Meiji Shrine, with its impressive torii gate, is another great place to escape the noisy crowds... From Shinjuku Station: Four minutes on the JR Yamanote Line.

claim: Roppongi pairs the foreigner-friendly nightlife reputation with the 'Art Triangle Roppongi' (National Art Center, Mori Art Museum, Suntory Museum of Art) plus the Roppongi Hills and Tokyo Midtown complexes; reached by Hibiya/Oedo/Nanboku lines (~10 min from Shinjuku).
quote: Roppongi has been a popular nightlife district among foreigners for decades... The 'Art Triangle Roppongi' features the National Art Center, Mori Art Museum, and Suntory Museum of Art... From Shinjuku Station: 10 minutes by direct Oedo Line.

claim: Shibuya is an entertainment district that 'warrants a late start' — peak pedestrian volume at the Crossing is 3–5 PM and the neighborhood transforms after dark; Harajuku-to-Shibuya is a 20-minute walk down Cat Street, making the two natural to chain in one afternoon-into-evening.
quote: Shibuya is a neighborhood that warrants a late start, as it is an entertainment district and comes alive at night... Peak pedestrian volume at the Shibuya Crossing occurs 3-5 PM... Harajuku to Shibuya is a 20-minute walk down Cat Street.

claim: Daikanyama and Nakameguro form a contiguous walking route of 'fashion, food and art vibes'; Daikanyama T-Site (Tsutaya Books) is the design-forward anchor, while Nakameguro's Meguro River canal walk is lined with boutique coffee, vintage shops, and indie restaurants.
quote: Ebisu, Daikanyama and Nakameguro — three neighboring neighborhoods beloved by young people and creatives — form one of Tokyo's trendiest areas... Daikanyama T-Site... blends cafés, music and stationery into a cultural hub.

claim: Nakameguro's lantern-lit Meguro River canal is the centerpiece of its after-dark scene — bars spill chairs onto the riverside path in summer, and the area feels like 'a good evening rather than a spectacle' versus Roppongi's tourist-heavy nightlife.
quote: The centerpiece of Nakameguro nightlife is the Meguro River—a narrow, lantern-lit canal that cuts through the neighborhood. In summer, bars put chairs and plants directly on the riverside path, and the whole thing becomes an outdoor living room for the neighborhood.

claim: Roppongi has a 'complicated reputation' — biggest international bar/club concentration but also the area most associated with tourist scams, overpriced cover charges, and aggressive touts, so visit with awareness.
quote: Roppongi has a complicated reputation. It's home to the largest concentration of international bars and clubs in Tokyo — and also the area most likely to involve tourist scams, overpriced cover charges, and aggressive touts.

claim: Tsukiji outer market shops open from around 5 AM and most close by 2 PM with the market closed Sundays and select Wednesdays; the sweet spot for breakfast is 8-10 AM.
quote: Most shops open around 5:00 AM and close by 2:00 PM, and the market is closed Sundays and select Wednesdays.

claim: Tsukiji signature tamagoyaki stalls Yamachou (sweeter, caramelised) and Shouro (more savoury, dashi-forward) are the two best-known egg-omelette shops in the outer market.
quote: Yamachou's version is sweeter with a caramelized exterior, while Shouro's is more savory with a prominent dashi flavor.

claim: Maguroya Kurogin is a tiny Tsukiji outer-market stall famous for fresh tuna cuts with a long but fast-moving line; Kitsuneya serves horumon-ni (offal stew) for adventurous eaters.
quote: Maguroya Kurogin is a small stall for fresh tuna cuts that's always crowded, though the line moves very fast.

claim: Tokyo's 2026 ramen top tier still includes Ichiran (tonkotsu), Nakiryu (Michelin Bib), Tsuta and Kipposhi; the year's breakout is Chuka Soba Kamofuku (opened May 2024, Tabelog 3.93).
quote: Chūka Soba Kamofuku opened on May 15, 2024, and has already shot up to the top 10 on Tabelog Tokyo's ramen rankings with an impressive 3.93 rating!

claim: Tsuta — the first-ever Michelin-starred ramen shop — closed in September 2022 after chef Yuki Onishi's death and reopened in February 2023 in Yoyogi-Uehara, Shibuya Ward.
quote: Tsuta closed in September 2022... The restaurant reopened on February 10th, 2023 in the Yoyogi-Uehara neighborhood of Tokyo's Shibuya Ward.

claim: Omoide Yokocho is a 100-metre L-shaped alley on Shinjuku station's west side with about 80 tiny counter-only yakitori, ramen and motsu-nabe joints, skewers at ¥100-200 and a full meal around ¥2,000-3,000.
quote: Skewers are still ¥100–200. A full meal with drinks is ¥2,000–3,000 — cheaper than a chain izakaya in Shinjuku.

claim: Ebisu Yokocho is a covered retro alley of 21 small counters minutes from Ebisu station, founded in 2008, with most stalls opening at 5 PM and running until 4 AM, around ¥2,000 per person.
quote: The collective of 21 small food counters cum watering holes is known as Ebisu Yokocho.

claim: Isetan Shinjuku's B1 depachika is rated the gold standard in Tokyo, with in-store sake/whisky sommeliers, ornate bento, wagashi, and outposts of Pierre Hermé and Jean-Paul Hévin.
quote: in-store sommeliers selling boutique sake and top-shelf Japanese whisky, as well as ornate bento boxes, a wide selection of intricate wagashi (traditional Japanese sweets), stores by revered French patisserie Pierre Herme and chocolatier Jean-Paul Hevin.

claim: Themed-cafe quality is uneven; ethical owl cafes like Akiba Fukurou meet a five-point welfare checklist (lighting, no tethering, optional handling, vet statement, ≤2 guests per active bird) while many Harajuku/Asakusa venues do not.
quote: Akiba Fukurou meets all five; many Harajuku and Asakusa venues do not.

claim: Uobei in Shibuya runs a non-revolving triple-lane bullet-train delivery system; Sushiro is the largest chain in Japan but central Shinjuku/Shibuya branches have long queues, so Ikebukuro is recommended instead.
quote: A hybrid Genki/Uobei flagship opened in October 2025 in Ueno Gate that ditches the traditional belt in favor of bullet-train-style express lanes that deliver your order directly to your seat moments after you tap the touchscreen.

claim: Uogashi Nihonichi is a tachigui (standing) sushi bar 3-4 minutes from Shinjuku west exit with pieces from ¥162 (maguro, ebi, tamago) to ¥432 (ikura, unagi), about 15 customers at a time, English menu available.
quote: grab some maguro ika, ebi, anago, or tamago sushi at JPY162... while aji, salmon, and yaki-salmon-mayo come at JPY216... and hotate, unagi, and ikura go at JPY432.

claim: Shinjuku Gyoen charges 500 JPY adult admission, opens 9:00–16:30 (last entry 16:00), closed Mondays, with seasonal extended hours during cherry blossom season.
quote: Admission is 500 JPY for adults, with discounted rates for students and free entry for children under age 15. Gates typically open from 9:00 a.m. to 4:30 p.m., with the last entry at around 4:00 p.m.

claim: Rikugien Garden is open 9:00–17:00 with 300 yen admission, extended to 20:30 during autumn illumination (late November) and cherry blossom season; built ~1700, recreates 88 poetic scenes.
quote: Regular Hours: 9:00 AM to 5:00 PM (entry until 4:30 PM) Evening Hours: Until 8:30 PM during autumn colors and cherry blossoms... Admission: 300 yen... 'reproduces in miniature 88 scenes from famous poems.'

claim: Hamarikyu Gardens open 9:00–17:00 daily (last entry 16:30) for 300 yen, feature a tidal seawater pond and the Nakajima teahouse where matcha costs 500 yen or 1,000 yen with wagashi.
quote: The garden is open 9 AM to 5 PM daily (closed Dec 29–Jan 1)... Tickets cost ¥300 for adults... Tea at Nakajima-no-ochaya is 500 yen, though a matcha set with nerikiri (traditional wagashi) or dorayaki is 1,000 yen each.

claim: Tokyo's three Grand Sumo tournaments at Ryogoku Kokugikan in 2026 are January 11–25 (Hatsu), May 10–24 (Natsu), and September 13–27 (Aki); tickets range 2,200–14,800 yen.
quote: January Tournament (Hatsu Basho): January 11–25, 2026; May Tournament (Natsu Basho): May 10–24, 2026; September Tournament (Aki Basho): September 13–27, 2026... Tickets range from ¥2,200 for same-day unreserved standing tickets to ¥14,800 for premium ringside masu box seats.

claim: Kabukiza offers hitomakumi (single-act) tickets letting tourists watch one scene at an affordable price without committing to a full 4-hour program; pricing varies by act and is announced per month.
quote: Single act performances are known as 'hitomakumi' in Japanese, and you can choose to watch particular scenes at an affordable price within a short time, making it an ideal way to enjoy kabuki for both novices and experts, as well as tourists who want to save some of their time for sightseeing.

claim: Tokyo National Museum opens 9:30–17:00 (until 20:00 Fri/Sat) for 1,000 yen adult admission, with the Gallery of Horyuji Treasures and the country's largest collection of Japanese art.
quote: Hours: 9:30 a.m. – 5:00 p.m. with extended hours until 8:00 p.m. on Friday, Saturday, and Sundays preceding holidays... Adults: 1,000 yen... It features the 'Gallery of Horyuji Treasures', displays Japanese archaeology, and showcases Asian art.

claim: Mori Art Museum in Roppongi Hills opens 10:00–22:00 (last entry 21:30, until 17:00 Tuesdays), focusing on contemporary art with admission around 2,000 yen depending on exhibition.
quote: Hours: 10:00-22:00 (Last Admission: 21:30) * 10:00-17:00 on Tuesdays (Last Admission: 16:30)... Admission depends on the current exhibition but adults can expect to pay around 2000 yen.

claim: Edo-Tokyo Open Air Architectural Museum in Koganei displays 30 relocated historic buildings on 7 hectares, open 9:30–17:30 (Apr–Sep) or 16:30 (Oct–Mar), 400 yen adult, closed Mondays; inspired Miyazaki's Spirited Away.
quote: The museum is open April-September from 9:30 AM to 5:30 PM and October-March from 9:30 AM to 4:30 PM... Admission costs 400 yen for adults... features historic buildings of high cultural value relocated to a seven-hectare site within Koganei Park, with a total of 30 buildings currently displayed.

claim: Hie Shrine in Akasaka and Nezu Shrine in Bunkyo are major historic shrines far less crowded than Meiji or Senso-ji; Gotokuji is the maneki-neko birthplace and Sengakuji holds the 47 Ronin graves.
quote: Hie Shrine - Located on the hilltops between Akasaka and Nagatacho, Hie Shrine is one of Tokyo's major shrines — but it isn't nearly as busy as Sensoji or Meiji Shrine... Gotokuji Temple - Widely known as the birthplace of the lucky beckoning cat, or maneki-neko.

claim: Nezu Shrine's Azalea Festival peaks April 10–20 each year with 3,000 bushes and a small festival admission fee, and the shrine's red torii corridor evokes a mini Fushimi Inari.
quote: The Nezu Azalea Shrine Festival typically reaches peak bloom between April 10 and April 20... During the festival, the garden is open daily from 9:30 AM to 5:30 PM with a small admission fee.

claim: Thermae-Yu in Shinjuku is Tokyo's most accessible onsen (open 22 hours, real Izu hot-spring water, tattoo-tolerant with stickers); Daikoku-yu in Oshiage is a renovated 1949 sento with a Mt Fuji mural at ~550 yen.
quote: Thermae-Yu is undoubtedly one of the best onsen experiences in Tokyo... Open 22 hours every day... Daikoku-yu... has been open since 1949 and holds one of the best views in Tokyo bathing... With an entrance fee of only around 550 yen.

claim: Happo-en garden runs walk-in tea ceremony Sat/Sun/Mon 11:00–15:00 for 1,100 yen per person, in a 500-year-old bonsai garden; Hamarikyu hosts the annual Tokyo Grand Tea Ceremony each October.
quote: Happo-en Tea Ceremony... available only on Saturday, Sunday and Monday with opening hours from 11am – 3pm (no reservations accepted) for 1,100 yen per person... The Tokyo Grand Tea Ceremony takes place at Hamarikyū Gardens on October 4-5 in 2026.

claim: The National Noh Theatre near Sendagaya Station stages year-round Noh/Kyogen on a stage of 400-year-old cypress with English audio guide and built-in seat-back subtitle screens.
quote: The National Noh Theatre, located just a five-minute walk from Sendagaya Station, is the perfect place to watch Nogaku... all seats are very comfortable with built-in screens to display the words of the performances that allow you to pick your language... made from the wood of 400-year-old cypress trees.

claim: Tokyo's 2026 cherry blossoms are forecast to open March 19 and reach full bloom around March 27–29, several days earlier than average due to a warm February.
quote: In 2026, the cherry blossom dates in Tokyo are expected to start on March 19th and peak on March 27th, which is a few days earlier than average... Tokyo cherry blossoms are forecast to peak between March 26 and March 29, 2026.

claim: teamLab Borderless reopened at Azabudai Hills Garden Plaza B B1 in Minato-ku in February 2024 and remains the official location as of 2026.
quote: [Official] teamLab Borderless TOKYO, Azabudai Hills

claim: teamLab Borderless Azabudai Hills tickets start from ¥3,800 and the venue operates 8:30–21:00 with weekend slots regularly selling out.
quote: Borderless at Azabudai Hills tickets start from ¥3,800... Tickets for teamLab Borderless Azabudai Hills sell out, especially for popular weekend slots.

claim: teamLab Planets TOKYO in Toyosu sells timed-entry tickets via its official DMM-run store, with adult tickets from ¥3,200.
quote: teamLab Planets TOKYO Official Ticket Store - Entrance tickets sales

claim: teamLab Planets and Borderless both routinely sell out weekend/morning slots, with booking at least two weeks ahead strongly advised.
quote: Both venues require advance tickets and both sell out frequently. You should book at least two weeks early.

claim: Shibuya Sky online tickets cost ¥2,500 (¥3,000 at the counter), with sunset slots releasing exactly 28 days before at 00:00 JST and disappearing within minutes.
quote: The 2026 adult fare is ¥2,500 online and ¥3,000 at the counter... Open the booking page at 23:55 Japan time exactly 28 days before your date, refresh at 00:00, and complete checkout in under 90 seconds — popular sunset slots in cherry blossom season vanish in two minutes.

claim: Tokyo City View at Roppongi Hills Mori Tower has the open-air Sky Deck rooftop closed since April 2024 and the indoor deck has partial closures into 2026.
quote: [NOTICE] Closure of the Sky Deck | Tokyo City View

claim: Tokyo City View on the Mori Tower 52nd floor remains open with 11 m floor-to-ceiling glass and tickets around ¥1,800.
quote: Tokyo City View

claim: Akihabara remains Tokyo's otaku capital for anime, manga, gaming and electronics; access via the JR Yamanote 'Electric Town Exit', with Chuo-dori pedestrianised Sunday afternoons.
quote: Akihabara, also known as Akihabara Electric Town, is Tokyo's ultimate otaku district, globally recognized as the capital of anime, manga, and gaming culture... Sunday afternoons (12:00–18:00) provide a unique festival atmosphere as Chuo-dori closes to vehicles.

claim: Key Akihabara stops include Yodobashi Akiba (electronics), Radio Kaikan, Mandarake (secondhand anime/manga) and Super Potato (retro gaming) alongside arcades and maid cafes.
quote: Key destinations include Yodobashi Akiba for electronics, Akihabara Radio Kaikan for specialty retailers, Mandarake for secondhand anime and manga, and Super Potato for retro gaming.

claim: Nakano Broadway, five minutes by JR Chuo from Shinjuku, packs 300+ shops across four floors and is Mandarake's birthplace, holding the densest collection of rare anime/manga goods in Tokyo.
quote: Nakano Broadway is a multi-story shopping complex five minutes from Shinjuku on the JR Chuo Line. Inside, it's a vertical maze of over 300 shops across four floors, with the highest concentration of rare anime and manga goods anywhere in Tokyo.

claim: Daily Chico in Nakano Broadway's basement serves a famous 40 cm eight-flavour soft-serve tower for ¥1,000, with most shops open 12:00–20:00.
quote: Daily Chico is the legendary ice cream stand in the basement. Their signature item is the Tokudai Soft Cream — an eight-flavor tower standing about 40 centimeters tall. It costs ¥1,000

claim: Takeshita Street is a 350–400 m pedestrian strip from JR Harajuku Station's Takeshita Exit to Meiji-dori packed with ~130 kawaii fashion shops, crepes (¥400–800) and themed cafes.
quote: Takeshita Street (350 m, ~130 shops) draws huge crowds daily, with foreign tourists comprising 30–40% of visitors by 2024.

claim: Harajuku in 2026 is seeing a Y2K colour revival in youth street style, best experienced Sunday afternoons (people-watching) or 9 am Sundays (uncrowded photos).
quote: A big trend in 2025–2026 is 'ditching black'... A Y2K revival is in full swing – you'll spot throwback 2000s 'gal' fashion elements... If you're an early riser, Sunday mornings around 9 AM let you wander virtually alone.

claim: Pokémon Cafe TOKYO (Nihonbashi Takashimaya 5F) is closed for renovation from March 23, 2026 and reopens Wednesday June 17, 2026 with reservation-only entry and revised 10:30–21:00 hours.
quote: We are pleased to announce the reopening date of Pokémon Cafe TOKYO!

claim: Pokémon Cafe is reservation-only via reserve.pokemon-cafe.jp, with slots released 31 days before the visit at 6 pm JST and selling out within minutes.
quote: Reservation page for Pokémon Cafe TOKYO... Reservations are released every day at 6pm, 31 days before the day of visiting.

claim: Ghibli Museum (Mitaka) is advance-reservation only via Lawson Ticket; tickets release at 10:00 JST on the 10th of each month for the following month, with adult entry ¥1,000 and four daily entry slots.
quote: No reservation or ticket purchase can be made at the Museum... New monthly tickets go on sale at 10 a.m. JST on the 10th of each month for the following month... Ages 19+: 1,000

claim: Ghibli Park is in Nagakute, Aichi (~50 min east of Nagoya) — a half-day-plus round trip from Tokyo, not realistic for a single weekend visitor focused on Tokyo.
quote: GHIBLI PARK

claim: Ghibli Park tickets release at 14:00 JST on the 10th two months before visit, range ¥1,000–¥7,800 across five areas, are non-refundable and require advance booking via Lawson/Klook.
quote: Ghibli Park tickets are released at 2:00 PM Japan Standard Time on the 10th of the month, two months before your intended visit... Ticket prices range from ¥1,000 ($7) for individual area passes to ¥7,800 ($53) for the Premium All-Area Pass on weekends.

claim: The original MariCar street-kart business shut after Nintendo's successful copyright suit, ending costume-as-Mario tours in Tokyo.
quote: Sorry, Mario Kart fans: Tokyo's IRL go-karting is no more

claim: Street Kart (formerly Mari Mobility) is the surviving licensed go-kart operator in Tokyo, runs Shibuya/Akihabara/Asakusa/Tokyo Bay routes and explicitly bans Nintendo costumes, requiring a valid driving licence recognised in Japan.
quote: [STREET KART Tokyo] Official Tokyo Go-kart Tour in Japan

claim: Kamakura is reachable in ~1 hour from Tokyo Station via JR Yokosuka Line for around ¥940 one way, with the Great Buddha (Kotoku-in), Hase-dera and Komachi-dori as headline draws.
quote: Travel costs ¥940 one way via the R Yokosuka Line from Tokyo Station to Kamakura Station. Don't miss the Great Buddha (Kotoku-in), the visually layered Hase-dera Temple with its ocean views, and the lively Komachi-dori shopping street.

claim: The Hakone Freepass gives unlimited use of Odakyu trains, buses, boats, cablecars and ropeways for 2-3 days; if bought without the Romance Car upgrade, regular round-course tickets would exceed ¥8,000 making the pass pay off.
quote: The Hakone Freepass provides unlimited use of Odakyu-affiliated buses, trains, boats, cablecars and ropeways in the Hakone area and discounted admission to selected tourist attractions on two or three consecutive days.

claim: The Odakyu Romancecar limited express from Shinjuku reaches Hakone-Yumoto in around 80 minutes direct with no transfers; a Romance Car seat reservation costs an extra ~¥1,200 on top of the Freepass.
quote: The Romancecar, Odakyu's limited express service, departs directly from Shinjuku and reaches Hakone-Yumoto in around 80 minutes with no transfers.

claim: Nikko's most economical access is the Tobu Limited Express Spacia X or Revaty from Asakusa, reaching Tobu-Nikko Station in roughly 1 hour 50 minutes; the Nikko Pass World Heritage Area (¥3,000, 2 days) bundles the round-trip train with unlimited local buses.
quote: The Nikko Pass World Heritage Area is valid for two consecutive days and allows you to travel freely within the world heritage area, which is centred around the spectacular Nikko Toshogu Shrine.

claim: The Fuji Excursion limited express runs direct Shinjuku to Kawaguchiko in under 2 hours, three departures daily, ¥4,130 one way without a JR Pass; highway buses from Shinjuku/Tokyo/Shibuya take 2-2.5 hours at ¥2,000-2,600.
quote: In less than 2 hours, the Fuji Excursion train takes you from Tokyo's Shinjuku station to major tourist attractions around the Mount Fuji area... The price is 4,130 yen one way without a JR Pass

claim: A Tokyo Disneyland or DisneySea 1-Day Passport for 2026 uses date-based dynamic pricing of ¥7,900-¥10,900 adult; a limited-period summer Park-Hopper option (July 1 - Sept 14, 2026) lets guests switch parks from 11am.
quote: From July 1, 2026 through September 14, 2026, guests can select either Tokyo Disneyland or Tokyo DisneySea to start their day, and from 11:00 a.m., they can hop between the parks.

claim: Yanaka is one of the few Tokyo districts that survived the 1923 Great Kanto Earthquake and WWII air raids largely intact, preserving pre-war street layouts and low-rise architecture; Yanaka Ginza is a ~170m shotengai with ~70 small shops.
quote: These three districts are among the few parts of Tokyo that survived both the 1923 Great Kanto Earthquake and the WWII air raids, preserving their pre-war street layouts and low-rise architecture.

claim: Yanaka began as a temple town in the Edo Period centred on Tennoji and Kaneiji, and is nicknamed 'Cat Town' because Edo-era temples kept cats to control mice; Yanaka Cemetery contains the grave of last shogun Tokugawa Yoshinobu.
quote: Yanaka has been nicknamed Cat Town, and the reputation goes back to the Edo period when local temples kept cats to manage the mouse population.

claim: Shimokitazawa is Tokyo's bohemian quarter for vintage clothing, indie live houses and record stores; signature vintage shops include New York Joe Exchange, 2nd Street, Flamingo, Big Time, Haight & Ashbury and Ragtag.
quote: Popular stores include Flamingo, New York Joe Exchange, Big Time, Haight & Ashbury, and Ragtag, with each shop offering a unique selection of styles and eras.

claim: Shimokitazawa's reputation as Tokyo's indie music capital traces to low 1960s/70s rents that pulled artists out of gentrifying Shibuya and Shinjuku; key live houses include Shelter, Shimokitazawa Three and Era, and Flash Disc Ranch (run by Masao Tsubaki since 1982) anchors vinyl culture.
quote: In the 1960s and 1970s, the relatively low rents attracted young people from gentrifying enclaves in Shibuya and Shinjuku, and live music venues and bars soon followed, as did theatres and niche performance spaces, cementing Shimokita's artistic reputation.

claim: Golden Gai is a compact network of about 200 tiny bars in Shinjuku, each seating only 5-8 people, retaining post-war ambiance; expect a ¥500-¥1,500 seating charge plus ¥700-¥1,500 drinks, budget ¥3,000-¥5,000 for a 2-hour visit.
quote: Golden Gai is a compact network of around 200 tiny bars in Shinjuku that offers a rare glimpse into old Tokyo nightlife, with each venue seating as few as five to eight people.

claim: Golden Gai is about a 10-minute walk from Shinjuku Station's east exit; the best window is 9pm to midnight on a weekday (Tue-Thu) for atmosphere without weekend crowds.
quote: The best time to visit Golden Gai is between 9:00 PM and midnight on a weekday. Most bars open around 7:00 PM and reach their liveliest point by late evening.

claim: Kichijoji is regularly voted Tokyo's most desirable neighborhood to live in, anchored by Inokashira Park (boating lake, Benten Shrine, top cherry-blossom spot) with Harmonica Yokocho's standing bars and the Mitaka Ghibli Museum a 15-minute walk away.
quote: Kichijoji is often hailed as Tokyo's most desirable place to live, primarily because the vast and lovely Inokashira Park is just minutes away from Kichijoji Station.

claim: Koenji is the birthplace of Japanese punk rock from the late 1970s/early 1980s and remains a live-house hub; JIROKICHI (opened 1975) is one of Tokyo's first live houses and Koenji Junjo Shopping Street has around 250 antique and second-hand stores.
quote: Koenji was the birthplace of Japanese punk rock in the late 1970s and early 1980s... JIROKICHI opened in 1975 and is one of Tokyo's first live houses hosting performances every night across a range of genres.
